rv.q: But just as Randolph-Wright approaches salient critique, a gear shift in plot or conversation restricts “Duke & Roya” to its rom-com genre.
Duke & Roya is directed by Warren Adams with great nuance. Not a voice is raised without visible reason. The company is spectacularly good at listening.
Duke & Roya is a gripping drama that grapples with global issues through the soft lens of a love story.
Duke & Roya is both entertaining and appealing as an unpredictable romance in a war-torn country.
In these relentlessly troubled times, its story and final, cheering visual feel a balm.
Political observations are overshadowed by the treacly storyline with Duke using his wealth and influence to attempt to rescue Roya who wants to remain in Afghanistan and fight for women’s rights.
A mix of high points and mediocre ones, Duke & Roya is successful as a romantic drama but less so as political one.
The actual production, though, lands somewhere in-between pointed tale and romance, not completely satisfying as either, despite a charming four-member cast.
Despite spanning 2017 to 2025, Duke & Roya could use condensing, especially in the somewhat plodding Act 1...
A potentially powerful story is hobbled by its fidelity to genre conventions.
It’s too bad that “Duke & Roya” doesn’t offer its talented players, or the audience, more substance overall.
Duke & Roya is an absolute delight.
Randolph-Wright's real narrative gift is his ability to unearth what it means to not only love another, but love one's country and oneself.
Despite its flaws, Duke & Roya is a compelling and thoughtful romantic drama that showcases some star-worthy performances.

In Charles Randolph-Wright’s Duke & Roya, the chemistry goes beyond the molecular level, as Jay Ellis and Stephanie Nur demonstrate in the title roles. It’s a powerful component for this play, which by turns is romantic and political and covers a lot of ground without quite bursting at the seams.

Fair warning: Duke & Roya is slow. Transitions between scenes feel labored. But its design (Wilson Chin), lighting (Amina Alexander), and projections (Caite Hevner) are spare and attractive, and the performances are so well-observed, the humor so subtle, and the gentle slow-burn of romance, familial...

cn.t: Critics find this romantic drama buoyed by the sizzling chemistry between leads Jay Ellis and Stephanie Nur, though opinions split on whether the love story successfully meshes with its weighty Afghanistan war backdrop.

vr.q: If you love a good Romeo and Juliet from different worlds romance with a little bit of suspense thrown in there definitely go see this.
If you didn't make it to Duke & Roya at the Lortel before it reached its untimely early closing this past weekend, I wouldn't sweat it.
